### Why iterate? 

you will encounter problems where you need to wrtie the same basic code a lot  

### `for` loops 

loops are the easiest place to start: output object, sequence to iterate over, the loop body, and optionally an input object 
we might not use these loops for very long after learning them 

### Loop functions

loop process (supply input vector/list, apply function to each element, save the result to a vector/list) is very common 
for loops can get a little tedious and opaque --> loop functions clean this up. Use map functions

### map 

output = map(input, f) 
map across input, applying f function to each element, and spit out output 

### map variants 

by default, map takes one input and will return a list 
you can use specific map variants to help prevent errors and simplify outputs associated with what kind of output your function produces 

### workflow 

write single example for fixed inputs 
abstract example to a function 
(embed function in a loop) - can skip depending on how comfortable you are with map statement 
re-write using a map statement 

### Lists 

these provide a way to store collections of arbitrary size and type 
Can mix character vectors, numeric vectors, matrices, summaries 
Data frames are a special kind of list (each entry is a vector of same length. can still mix variable classes. printed as a table)

### list columns 

lists can contain anything, even another list --> this can be very useful in the context of iteration 
keeping everything in one dataframe with list columns means there are fewer things to worry about

## Lists 

Prove that lists can have anything 

```{r}
l = list(
  vec_numeric = 5:17, 
  mat = matrix(1:8, nrow = 2, ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE), 
  vec_logical = c(TRUE), 
  summary_table = summary(rnorm(1000))
)

l 

l[[1]]

l[[2]]

l[["vec_logical"]]

l$summary_table #don't do this, shorthand for brackets 
```

# `for` loops 

```{r}
# create input list first 
list_norm = list(
  a = rnorm(20, 3, 4),
  b = rnorm(20, -14, 20),
  c = rnorm(20, 1000, 1000),
  d  = rnorm(20, 0, 1)
) 
```

Can I get mean and sd for each sample?
Use function we wrote last time 

```{r}
mean_and_sd(list_norm[[1]])
mean_and_sd(list_norm[[2]])
mean_and_sd(list_norm[[3]])
mean_and_sd(list_norm[[4]])

# pull out specific item in list, then apply that function 
# already tedious to deal with four of these --> write a for loop! 
```

Doing this better with a for loop: 

```{r}
#define an empty list for a space for each output I care about, length = 4 because we're working with four variables  
output = vector("list", length = 4) 

for (i in 1:4) { #go through 1, 2, 3, 4, put outputs of function on list norm into new list called output
  
  output[[i]] = mean_and_sd(list_norm[[i]])
  
}

output #empty list you made is now filled with the output from the for loop 
```

## use `map` instead

Take for loop and modify it 

```{r}
output = map(list_norm, mean_and_sd) #where we save output = (input list, function I care about)
output = map(list_norm, median) #can use map and change what function you apply 

#regular map always gives you a list 
```

## Map variants 

```{r}
output = map_df(list_norm, median) #simplifying outputs if you want, putting into df 

output = map_dbl(list_norm, median) #putting in a vector, doesn't separate out into list
```

## list columns 

```{r}
listcol_df = 
  tibble(
    name = c("a", "b", "c", "d"), 
    samp = list_norm #this is a legit list we made 
  )

listcol_df
```
this will be a df and one of the columns will be a list, items in that column are collections of 20 numbers

do stuff with it 

```{r}
listcol_df |> 
  filter(name == "a")
```

```{r}
listcol_df |> 
  filter(name %in% c("a", "c", "d"))

listcol_df |> 
  pull(samp)
```

mean and sd 

```{r}
mean_and_sd(pull(listcol_df, samp)[[1]]) #this is ugly do not do this 
```

could i iterate?

```{r}
#pull(listcol_df, samp) #this is still an input list, iterate across this input list and apply mean and sd function and save result

map(pull(listcol_df, samp), mean_and_sd)
```
Jeff hates pulling stuff out of a df, ideally we would keep it in df and put results in another df 

do this instead: 
mutate to add a column
```{r}
listcol_df |> 
  mutate(
    output = map(samp, mean_and_sd) #adding output column, do map, mean/sd function across samp column, within listcol pipe  
  )

listcol_df |> 
  mutate(
    output = map_df(samp, mean_and_sd)
  ) #inside new column, there is a dataframe 

listcol_df |> 
  mutate(
    output = map_dbl(samp, median)
  )
```

## another example 

NSDUH import etc 

```{r}
nsduh_url = "https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/NSDUHsaeShortTermCHG2015/NSDUHsaeShortTermCHG2015.htm"

nsduh_html = read_html(nsduh_url)

nsduh_process(html = nsduh_html, table_num = 1)
nsduh_process(html = nsduh_html, table_num = 4)
nsduh_process(html = nsduh_html, table_num = 5)
```

import using iteration 

```{r}
output = vector("list", length = 3)

table_nums = c(1, 4, 5) #keeping track of which tables we care about, indexed i as 1:3 in for loop

for (i in 1:3) {
  
  output[[i]] = nsduh_process(html = nsduh_html, table_num = table_nums[i])
  
}

#gets a little confusing because output tables are now numbered differently than input tables, have to keep track 
```

Use map statements when you can on homeworks, not for loops!!! 

same process, import using map statement instead 

```{r}
map(table_nums, nsduh_process, html = nsduh_html) #what am i mapping across, what function am i doing, any additional arguments this function needs 
```
Exact same output! 

Now use list columns to do same thing 

```{r}
nsduh_df = 
  tibble(
    drug = c("marj", "cocaine", "heroin"), 
    num = c(1, 4, 5)
  ) |>  #want to add each output to a new column 
  mutate( 
    table = map(num, nsduh_process, html = nsduh_html)
    ) |> #adding column that maps across new num variable aka the tables, using the function and specifying the function argument 
  select(-num) |> 
  unnest(table) #unnest, expanding out all sub dataframes

nsduh_df |> 
  filter(age == "12-17") |> 
  mutate(State = fct_reorder(State, percent)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = State, y = percent, color = year)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(. ~ drug) #can also plot this stuff! 
```

### weather again? 

```{r}
data("weather_df") 

weather_df = 
  weather_df |> 
  nest(data = date:tmin) #takes everything and collapses 
```

What if i want to do a regression of tmax on tmin for each station?

```{r}
lm(tmax ~ tmin, data = pull(weather_df, data) [[1]]) #pulling first col from weather df, then run linear model on it 
lm(tmax ~ tmin, data = pull(weather_df, data) [[2]]) #second column (different station)
lm(tmax ~ tmin, data = pull(weather_df, data) [[3]]) 
```

```{r}
weather_lm = function(input_data) {
  
  lm(tmax ~ tmin, data = input_data)
  
}

weather_lm(pull(weather_df, data) [[1]]) #wrote a new function, applying to this data set 

# use map statement to fit lm function to each column of weather df, output in new col 

weather_df |> 
  mutate(
    lm_fits = map(data, weather_lm)
  ) |> 
  pull(lm_fits) #to check if it works, don't always have to do this 
```
